Long-term facilities are better suited to complete the full vaccine series, while short-term facilities should focus on initiating the series, providing immunization records, and offering discharge information about where remaining doses can be administered. 2. Vaccination can also be completed if the individual returns to a correctional institution. Pre-vaccination testing to detect existing immunity can reduce costs by avoiding unnecessary revaccination of individuals who were previously vaccinated or infected. 3. The Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) decided against pre-vaccination testing based on a model that considered the costs of testing and vaccination, as well as the completion rate of the vaccine series. The model assumed all inmates receiving the first dose would return for subsequent doses. However, if release-related attrition was factored in, pre-vaccination testing would only be cost-effective if immunity prevalence was high. 4. Changes in the prevalence of immunity to hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection or associated costs (e.g., vaccine, labor, and testing) could alter the cost-effectiveness of pre-vaccination testing. Immunity to HBV among young adults is rapidly changing due to increased vaccination rates among adolescents. 5. If adequate immunization records are unavailable for inmates, periodic monitoring of HBV immunity prevalence using serologic markers (e.g., anti-HBc for infection and antibodies to hepatitis B surface antigen for immunization) can help correctional officials determine when pre-vaccination testing might reduce costs. 6. The findings in this report are subject to limitations. First, inmates with shorter sentences are more likely to be discharged and may be overrepresented in the sampling. This could mean that more inmates completed the vaccine series than the study demonstrated, as those with shorter sentences may not have been incarcerated long enough to complete the series. 7. Second, the lack of long-term follow-up prevents evaluation of eventual vaccine series completion by jail inmates who may have accessed additional doses outside the correctional system or during subsequent incarcerations. 8. Hepatitis B vaccination of inmates in state correctional facilities is feasible if resources are available to purchase and administer the vaccine. A 2000 survey of state correctional facility medical directors indicated that most prison systems would vaccinate inmates if resources were available. 9. Despite recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination of inmates since the vaccine's introduction in 1982, only five states (Hawaii, Michigan, New Mexico, Vermont, and Wisconsin) routinely vaccinate inmates. Collaboration between public health and corrections authorities at state and local levels is essential to overcome barriers to implementing vaccination programs. 10. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has identified tuberculosis (TB) as a potential adverse reaction to treatment with tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) antagonists, such as infliximab (Remicade®), etanercept (Enbrel®), and adalimumab (Humira®). These products block TNF-α, an inflammatory cytokine, and are approved for treating rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases. 11. TNF-α plays a role in the immunology and pathophysiology of certain infectious diseases, notably TB. Blocking TNF-α can allow TB disease to emerge from latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. 12. In 2002, a California county health department reported three cases of TB disease associated with infliximab therapy. This report summarizes those cases and nine additional cases reported subsequently, providing interim recommendations for TB prevention and management in recipients of these blocking agents. 13. Healthcare providers should take steps to prevent TB in immunocompromised patients and remain vigilant for TB as a cause of unexplained febrile illness. 14. Case 1: A 55-year-old U.S.-born man with rheumatoid arthritis developed pulmonary TB 17 months after starting infliximab therapy. He had a history of a positive tuberculin skin test (TST) in 1995 and reportedly took isoniazid for 12 months, though adherence was questionable. After 13 infliximab infusions, he presented with fever, weight loss, and a right upper-lobe lung cavity. Mycobacterium tuberculosis was isolated, and his condition improved with anti-TB medications. However, he later developed lung cancer and died in November 2002. 15. Case 2: A 64-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis developed pulmonary and pericardial TB in June 2002 after receiving seven doses of infliximab. Drug-resistant TB was isolated, and her condition improved after 12 months of second-line anti-TB therapy. 16. Case 3: A 54-year-old U.S.-born woman with Crohn's disease developed TB after receiving infliximab. She had a history of a positive TST in 1996 but was not treated for latent TB infection. After her second infliximab infusion, she presented with cough, fever, and abdominal pain. Mycobacterium tuberculosis was isolated, and she was treated with a modified anti-TB regimen due to gastrointestinal intolerance, ultimately achieving disease resolution. 17. In 2003, the California Department of Health Services requested local jurisdictions to report TB cases associated with TNF-α antagonists. By September 2003, nine additional cases were reported. Most patients had at least one risk factor for latent TB infection, such as being born in a TB-prevalent country or contact with a person with TB disease. Many were also on other immunosuppressive therapies at the time of their TB diagnoses.
